sm: Matt Walsh opens by noting that Thanksgiving is almost here, so he wants to talk about Thanksgiving food. He argues that food has gotten worse across the board, and that holiday dinners are no exception. He starts with dessert, insisting that pie belongs on the big holidays instead of cake, and he spends a while mocking cake as forgettable and the birthday candle ritual as unsanitary.

He then turns to store-bought pumpkin pie, which he says is a step below homemade because of prepackaged ingredients and additives that keep the crust from going soggy. His main complaint is that most canned pumpkin pie filling contains little actual pumpkin and is instead a type of squash. He cites an FDA compliance policy dating to 1938 under which squash may be labeled pumpkin, so long as there is no evidence consumers are misled. Walsh calls this fraud, saying nearly every pumpkin pie sold at this time of year is mislabeled, though he concedes people mostly never noticed or complained.

Walsh cites a blind taste test from a 2017 magazine, where a pie made from true pumpkin scored lowest while squash-based pies did well. He says his point is not that squash pies are bad, but that the labeling is deceptive, and he jokes about which brands to avoid. He then moves to stuffing, reading an article about a boxed stuffing mix containing high fructose corn syrup and preservatives.

One preservative, BHA, is banned or restricted in places like the U.K., the EU, and Japan. He notes the FDA has recently launched a reassessment of it, and describes older studies finding tumors in the stomachs of rats, mice, and hamsters. He says there is no definitive finding in humans and that you would have to eat an enormous amount, but it is worth watching.

Next is the turkey. Walsh says modern turkeys are bred to be far heavier than heritage birds, averaging nearly thirty pounds by 2012, and are so large they cannot mate naturally. Even birds labeled all natural may contain up to eight percent of a salt water solution, listed only in small print. He cites taste testers who preferred heritage turkey, and a 2001 newspaper article describing salty, processed-tasting meat.

He explains that the USDA treats the injected solution as an added ingredient rather than water, which lets companies call the bird all natural while burying the disclosure. He also guesses the extra water may contribute to deep fryer accidents at this time of year. He jokes that people should forget the deep fryer and let a family member's home burn down instead, then begins talking about how many household things now depend on electricity.

Walsh says that seventy years ago deceptive food labeling was not an issue, and that the practice of misleading consumers really took off in the 1980s. He gives examples of products whose large front label names one thing while small print reveals another, comparing it to a roll of tape labeled as one product that is actually a different one. His main example is the yam, citing an LSU AgCenter article. Louisiana producers of moist, orange sweet potatoes wanted to distinguish them from drier white varieties, so they adopted the word yam, which actually names a different plant.

He jokes that the people responsible might deserve arrest, then says he is obliged to end on a note of optimism. Despite the deception, he says it has never been a better time to cook high quality meals at home. He plays a clip of a product demo in which an AI assistant walks someone through making a Korean-inspired steak sauce and gets steps confused, and he jokes that AI will eventually try to kill everyone by sabotaging recipes.

He jokes about asking AI for a Chinese chicken stir fry, then clarifies that his bleach and cyanide joke was only a joke. He suggests the whole turkey situation was a gigantic salty, watery scam. He imagines a future where nobody needs to cook or visit a supermarket, and with a sarcastic tone says AI will end humanity soon after, so people should just enjoy their meal with family while they can. He closes by wishing everyone a happy Thanksgiving.
sg: Fake Pumpkin, Stuffing, and Salty Turkey
